extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and advanced students in analytic geometry and classical mechanics (readers of a 19th-century mathematical journal)
extracted.subtask_description: Determine the species (ellipse, hyperbola, parabola) and special circular sections of plane sections of second-degree surfaces (quadrics), and related analytic criteria and constructions (including chords of contact, common tangents, and related theorems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion (8): sign of AC — B² determines species of plane section
rubrics_metrics.description: For a plane section with quadratic form Ay² + 2Byz + Cz² + ... = 0, the sign of (AC — B²) determines the species: positive => ellipse, negative => hyperbola, zero => parabola.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A, B, C are the coefficients of the quadratic terms after substituting the plane; compute A, B, C as derived from the surface coefficients and the directing cosines of the plane's normal. The text notes this is a 'very simple criterion' and applies whether axes are rectangular or (with appropriate substitution of coefficients proportional to L, M, N) oblique. Examples and discussion: for central surfaces with all principal coefficients positive the criterion is always positive (ellipsoid), while for hyperboloids or cones the terms can give any sign so all three section types may occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: General discriminant criterion (10) for arbitrary quadratic form
rubrics_metrics.description: For the general quadratic surface Avx² + A'y² + A''z² + 2Bxy + 2Byz + 2Bzx + ... = 0, the section made by any plane is classified by the value of a specific combination (given as formula (10)): if the combination is positive the section is an ellipse, if negative an hyperbola, if zero a parabola.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formula (10) is the discriminant-like expression built from the coefficients (A_i, B_ij) and the directing cosines (or proportional L,M,N) of the cutting plane. The same sign rules as in (8) apply. The page provides the explicit algebraic combination and comments on substituting L,M,N when these are proportional to the normal's cosines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution of plane coefficients L, M, N for directing cosines
rubrics_metrics.description: If the cutting plane is given by Lx + My + Nz = P' where L, M, N are proportional (but not normalized) to the directing cosines l, m, n of the normal, the proportional values L, M, N may be used in the discriminant criteria instead of the normalized cosines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The note emphasizes that since l, m, n are proportional to L, M, N, the latter can be substituted into the criteria (8) and (10) after appropriate proportional adjustment; this allows application when the plane is specified by its equation rather than by unit cosines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipsoid sections always ellipses (sign condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: If all principal coefficients (P1, P2, P3) of the central quadratic surface are positive, then the discriminant (8) is always positive and never zero, so every plane section is an ellipse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an immediate corollary of criterion (8). The page explicitly refers to central surfaces and notes the impossibility of the discriminant vanishing in this positive-coefficient case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperboloids and cone admit all three section species
rubrics_metrics.description: When one or two of the principal coefficients P1,P2,P3 are negative (as in the two hyperboloids and the cone), the discriminant (8) may be positive, negative, or zero; therefore such surfaces may be cut by a plane in an ellipse, hyperbola, or parabola.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains sign patterns: one positive and two negative terms (or vice versa) cause the discriminant to take any sign. This explains the diversity of plane sections for these surfaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paraboloids and elliptic/hyperbolic cylinders: one coefficient zero => parabolic/elliptic/hyperbolic sections
rubrics_metrics.description: If exactly one of the principal coefficients P1,P2,P3 is zero (e.g., P1 = 0), then sections by planes parallel to the axis corresponding to that zero coefficient are parabolas; other plane sections vary: for elliptic paraboloid and elliptic cylinder most other sections are ellipses, while for hyperbolic paraboloid and hyperbolic cylinder they are hyperbolas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When one coefficient is zero substitute into (8) (result (8') in text) and examine signs of the remaining coefficients. The special case 7 = 0 (cosine along axis = 0) makes (8') vanish, producing parabolas. The page clarifies these geometric correspondences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parabolic cylinder sections always parabolas or pair of parallel lines
rubrics_metrics.description: If two of the principal coefficients are zero (parabolic cylinder), the discriminant (7) always vanishes, so plane sections are all parabolas or a system of two parallel straight lines (considered as parabolas of infinite radius).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes the degenerate case (parallel straight lines) as a variety of the parabola, and explains it directly from the vanishing discriminant when two coefficients are zero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circular section criterion via symmetric coordinate transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Circular sections occur when, after a suitable orthogonal change of coordinates making the cutting-plane-parallel coordinate plane, the coefficients of y'² and z'² are equal and the coefficient of y'z' is zero. This leads to algebraic conditions (equations (11)-(19)) and ultimately to two plane families (equations (21) and (22)) whose parallels produce circular sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The method: choose transformed axes so that the plane yz is parallel to a circular section; require equality of coefficients of the two squared transverse coordinates and vanishing cross-term. Solve the resulting system in terms of principal coefficients P1,P2,P3 and the directing cosines of the new axes. The page derives explicit plane equations (21),(22) for the two series of circular sections and discusses when these series actually produce circles (they fail when the corresponding coefficient vanishes, producing straight-line sections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence and degeneracy conditions for circular sections
rubrics_metrics.description: The two series of circular sections exist in general but require the relevant mean P̄ (notation P̄ or P_i') to be nonzero. Hyperbolic paraboloid and hyperbolic/parabolic cylinders with P̄ = 0 have no true circular sections but instead give straight-line (degenerate) sections. The surfaces of revolution arise when the two families coincide (P1 = P2 or P̄ = P_i), and the sphere when all principal coefficients are equal (P1 = P2 = P3), in which case the circular-section planes become indeterminate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains how vanishing of the mean or equality of principal coefficients changes the geometry: zero mean -> degenerate straight-line 'circles' of infinite radius; equal coefficients -> coincidence of the two series -> axisymmetry or sphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Note: criteria valid for oblique axes with substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Although initial criteria (8) and (10) are established assuming rectangular axes, they remain true when axes are oblique provided l, m, n continue to denote the cosines of angles made by the normal with the axes, and one substitutes the coefficients L, M, N in place of normalized cosines when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author remarks that the analogous algebraic derivations for oblique axes are not entered upon here but asserts the validity of the criteria under the corresponding substitutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statical moments theorem for three coplanar forces
rubrics_metrics.description: If three forces acting in the same plane are in equilibrium, and from any point in that plane perpendiculars are drawn to the directions of the three forces, then the rectangle contained by the resultant and its perpendicular equals the sum or difference of the rectangles contained by the component forces and their respective perpendiculars, according as the chosen point is without or within the angle formed by the component force directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The note includes derivation using coordinates on a parallelogram and gives the formulaic relations (perpendicular distances times forces). The text warns that the theorem is incompletely stated in several works and clarifies the sign convention depending on point location relative to the angle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Galbraith's astronomical refraction formula (operational criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practical formula for astronomical refraction up to 85° zenith distance: r = √(1 + 14.5R'a tan(θ − 3°.375R'a tan θ) ... ) (given as formula (1) with specified constants and reductions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variables and constants are explicitly listed (R' = 206264''.8, coefficient a = 0.0000283 at 45°, barometer and temperature reductions, etc.). The page provides worked examples and compares the formula with Ivory's table, gives a reduced simpler form for certain ranges, and supplies computational constants and logs for practical use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for reality/imaginarity of imaginary exponentials (Propositions I–VI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several propositions give conditions under which expressions involving powers with imaginary base/exponent (e.g., (−1)^{...}, (a + b√−1)^m, (−k)^a etc.) are real or imaginary. Notable cases: (1) if k is positive and a any real number the expression is real; (2) when k is negative and a an integer or a fraction with odd denominator the expression is real; (3) with even denominators the expression is imaginary; (4) for more general infinite-series-generating a the character may depend on the generating function; and other propositions assert that (a + b√−1)^m is generally imaginary for real m and give algebraic conditions for reality (e.g., ab1 + a1b = 0 in one derived condition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text provides expanded discussion and several example cases (Props I–VII), including binomial expansions, reduction to trigonometric forms, and remarks on infinite series and ambiguities of parity in infinite expansions. Use the listed propositions as case taxonomy for whether such complex exponentials evaluate to real or imaginary values in given parameter combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for deriving chord of contact from conic and tangent equations
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a conic ay² + 2bxy + cx² + ... = 0 and a tangent at (x1,y1), combine the conic equation and the tangent equation to form a locus that contains the points of contact; subtracting the original conic yields the equation of the chord of contact corresponding to the given external point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page gives the algebraic combination: form a new curve combining the conic and tangent coefficients so that common points are the points of contact, then eliminate to get the chord of contact. Examples: for a circle the locus is a circle whose centre is the midpoint of the line joining the given point and the given circle's centre; for an ellipse the points of contact lie on a similarly situated ellipse whose centre is midway between the given point and the given ellipse centre. The method is claimed as novel by the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties of chord-of-contact loci for circle, ellipse, hyperbola
rubrics_metrics.description: For a circle, the curve containing points of contact of tangents from an external point is itself a circle whose centre is the midpoint of the segment joining the given point to the circle's centre and with radius √(p² + a²) (as derived). For an ellipse (and similarly hyperbola) the points of contact of two tangents from a given point lie on a similar ellipse passing through the given point and the centre, with centre midway between the given point and the given conic's centre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are explicit geometric properties deduced from the chord-of-contact construction; the page provides coordinates and reductions showing the centres and radii/parameters of the resulting locus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equation and enumerative criterion for common tangents to two circles
rubrics_metrics.description: A general algebraic equation (given as equation (23)) produces up to four common tangents to two circles; the number of real tangents is determined by combinations of radii p1,p2 and centre distance d: (1) intersecting circles (|p1 − p2| < d < p1 + p2) yield two common tangents (two real, two imaginary); (2) one circle wholly inside another (d < |p1 − p2|) yields no common tangents; (3) externally tangent circles (d = p1 + p2) yield two tangents (one pair coalesces); (4) internally tangent circles (d = |p1 − p2|) yield one tangent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The derivation sets up tangency conditions for unknown contact points on each circle and enforces identical tangent line equations (differing only by scale), leading to algebraic relations. The discriminants R² = d² − (p1 − p2)² and R² = d² − (p1 + p2)² appear and determine which cases give real solutions. Additional geometric conclusions: intersections of tangent pairs lie on the line joining centres or on its perpendicular depending on sign choices in the algebraic solution.
